bull.b: Early efficacy, safety and pharmacokinetic findings suggest TH103 may provide durable retinal benefit and less frequent dosing than existing therapies. If confirmed in later trials, this could support meaningful differentiation and improve the program’s competitive positioning.

Progression into a Phase 1b/2 study demonstrates operational execution beyond initial proof-of-concept. Continued patient dosing and manufacturing readiness create a path toward dose selection and later-stage development, supporting the value of the lead program.

Minimal debt reduces interest and refinancing pressure while the company funds clinical development. Although the balance sheet is shrinking, low leverage preserves flexibility and avoids the added obligations that can constrain highly indebted development-stage biotechs.

bear.b: Kalaris has no commercial revenue base to offset research, development and operating costs. Its financial outlook therefore remains dependent on clinical success, future financing or partnerships, leaving the business exposed until a product can be commercialized.

Sustained negative operating and free cash flow indicates that clinical progress requires continuing external funding. A slightly worsening burn rate can increase dilution or financing risk and may limit development flexibility if capital markets or partnership access weakens.

The steady reduction in equity reflects cumulative losses and cash consumption, weakening the company’s financial cushion. This erosion raises the importance of successful financing or clinical milestones and reduces resilience against delays, trial setbacks or higher development costs.
